specPoints.text: explain the uses of aluminium, copper, iron and steel in terms of their properties the types of steel will be limited to low-carbon (mild), high-carbon and stainless

primer.text: From Extraction & Uses of Metals you have seen how metals are won from their ores. Choosing which metal to use then comes down to matching properties to the job: conducting heat or electricity, resisting corrosion, staying non-toxic and keeping costs low. This note maps the uses of aluminium, copper, iron and steel onto exactly those properties.

lessons.title: Uses of aluminium and copper
lessons.opening: Aluminium and copper earn their places by conduction. Aluminium combines low density with strength, conducts heat and electricity well, and shrugs off acidic food, so it appears in aircraft, saucepans, overhead cables and food cans. Copper conducts electricity and heat, is easily worked, and does not react with water, which suits it to wiring, saucepans and water pipes.
keyPoints: Aluminium's low density and high strength make it ideal for aircraft bodies.
Aluminium is unreactive and shrugs off acidic foodstuffs, so it is used for food cans.
Overhead electrical cables use aluminium because it conducts electricity very well.
Copper's conductivity and ductility make it the standard choice for electrical wiring.
Water pipes rely on copper being unreactive with water, non-toxic and malleable.

low.restatement: Pick the metal by matching its properties to the job: aluminium is light and conducts, so it flies in aircraft and carries electricity; copper conducts and is easily shaped, so it wires houses and carries water.
low.analogy: Choosing a metal is like choosing a tool from a toolbox: the screwdriver goes to screws, the hammer to nails, and each metal goes to the use its properties fit.
low.examPointer: Answers need the pairing visible: name the use, then the property, in that order, for each metal.

medium.restatement: Aluminium earns aircraft bodies through its high strength-to-weight ratio, saucepans through heat conduction and unreactivity, cables through electrical conduction and cans through resistance to acidic food. Copper is chosen for wiring because it conducts and is ductile, for saucepans because it conducts heat and is malleable, and for water pipes because it stays unreactive, non-toxic and workable.
medium.analogy: Treat each use as a job advert: the properties are the candidate's skills, and only the metal whose skills match the advert gets the job.
medium.examPointer: Tables of uses against properties are common exam art, so practise reading both directions: use to property and property to use.

check.stem: Why is aluminium chosen for aircraft bodies?

options.text: Its high strength-to-weight ratio, coming from strength combined with low density
options.explanation: Strong but light is exactly what an airframe needs, which is the property listed for aircraft bodies.

options.text: It conducts electricity better than any other metal
options.explanation: Conductivity matters for cables, but the airframe property is strength at low weight.

options.text: It is the cheapest metal available
options.explanation: Cost is not the listed reason; strength with low density is.
options.misconception: cost substituted for the stated property

options.text: It is completely unreactive in every situation
options.explanation: Aluminium is useful because it resists specific attack such as acidic food, not because it never reacts.

check.stem: Which set of properties makes copper suitable for water pipes?

options.text: Unreactive with water, non-toxic and malleable
options.explanation: These are exactly the three properties listed for water pipes.

options.text: Low density and high strength
options.explanation: Those are aircraft properties for aluminium; pipes need chemical stability and workability.
options.misconception: aluminium properties transferred to copper pipes

options.text: Hardness and a high melting point
options.explanation: Neither property is the listed reason; the pipe must not react with water and must be safe and workable.

options.text: Magnetism and low cost
options.explanation: Copper is not magnetic and cost is not the listed property set.

check.stem: Which shared property puts both aluminium and copper into saucepans?

options.text: Both are very good conductors of heat
options.explanation: Heat conduction is listed for both metals in the saucepan row.

options.text: Both are ductile enough to be drawn into wires
options.explanation: Ductility is the wiring property; saucepans need heat conduction.

options.text: Both are strongly magnetic
options.explanation: Neither metal is magnetic, and magnetism has no role in cooking.

options.text: Both are the cheapest metals on sale
options.explanation: Cost is not the listed property; conduction of heat is.

check.stem: Why is aluminium suitable for food cans?

options.text: It is non-toxic and resists corrosion and acidic foodstuffs
options.explanation: The food-can row lists non-toxic behaviour plus resistance to corrosion and acidic foods.

options.text: It conducts electricity so it keeps food warm
options.explanation: Conductivity does not keep food warm and is not the listed reason.

options.text: It is denser than most metals so it seals tightly
options.explanation: Aluminium is prized for low density; the can property is chemical resistance.

options.text: It is magnetic so cans are easy to sort
options.explanation: Sorting convenience is not the listed reason and aluminium is not magnetic.
options.misconception: recycling habit mistaken for the property

check.stem: Which metal is used for overhead electrical cables, and why?

options.text: Aluminium, because it conducts electricity well and is light
options.explanation: Cables need a good conductor that a pylon can support, and aluminium supplies both.

options.text: Copper, because it is cheaper per metre
options.explanation: Copper wires houses, but overhead cables use aluminium for its conduction at low weight.

options.text: Iron, because it is strong in tension
options.explanation: Strength alone does not qualify; the cable must conduct electricity well.

options.text: Stainless steel, because it resists weathering
options.explanation: Weathering resistance is not the deciding property for the cable conductor.

lessons.title: Uses of iron and steel
lessons.opening: Iron provides cheap strength for building and, less centrally to this course, works as a catalyst. Steel, its alloy with carbon, comes in three named types: mild steel with a low carbon content is soft and malleable for car body panels, high-carbon steel is hard enough for tools such as chisels, and stainless steel resists corrosion in cutlery, sinks and chemical plants.
keyPoints: Iron is used as a building material because it is strong, malleable, ductile and relatively cheap.
Mild steel contains about 0.25% carbon and is soft and malleable, suiting car body panels.
High-carbon steel holds 0.5-1.4% carbon and is hard enough for tools such as chisels.
Stainless steel mixes in 20% chromium and 10% nickel, giving strength and corrosion resistance.
The carbon content decides the character of the steel, from soft and workable to hard.

low.restatement: Iron gives cheap strength for buildings, and steel tunes that strength by changing what is mixed into it: mild steel, with a little carbon, bends easily for body panels; high-carbon steel stays hard for cutting tools; and stainless steel, with chromium and nickel, shrugs off rusting in kitchens, sinks and chemical plants.
low.analogy: Steel types are like bread doughs: more flour, meaning more carbon, makes a stiffer loaf, so the bake is chosen for the job it must do, and special ingredients suit special jobs.
low.examPointer: Learn all three steel types with one use each; matching type to use is a classic one-mark question, and the percentages act as clues.

medium.restatement: Iron serves as an inexpensive building material with good strength, malleability and ductility, and steel is iron deliberately alloyed with carbon or other elements to tune its behaviour. Mild steel, near 0.25% carbon, stays soft for panels; high-carbon steel hardens into tools; stainless steel, with chromium and nickel added, resists corrosion in demanding settings.
medium.analogy: Think of alloying as tuning a recipe: a pinch of carbon softens the character for panels, a larger measure hardens it for chisels, and special ingredients make it survive the sink.
medium.examPointer: Percentages appear in questions as clues: 0.25% means mild, 0.5-1.4% means high-carbon, and chromium plus nickel means stainless.

check.stem: Which type of steel is used for car body panels, and why?

options.text: Mild steel, because it is soft and malleable
options.explanation: Body panels must be pressed into shape, which needs the soft, workable character of low-carbon mild steel.

options.text: High-carbon steel, because panels must be hard
options.explanation: Hardness suits chisels and tools; panels need to be shaped, which mild steel does best.

options.text: Stainless steel, because panels must not rust
options.explanation: Corrosion resistance is the stainless property for cutlery and sinks; panels use mild steel's workability.

options.text: Pure iron, because alloys weaken metals
options.explanation: Car panels use mild steel; alloying is done deliberately to tune properties, not always to weaken.

check.stem: Which steel type suits tools such as chisels?

options.text: High-carbon steel, which is hard
options.explanation: Cutting edges need hardness, and the 0.5-1.4% carbon content provides exactly that.

options.text: Mild steel, which is soft and malleable
options.explanation: A soft chisel would deform on impact; hardness is the required property.

options.text: Stainless steel, which resists corrosion
options.explanation: Corrosion resistance matters for cutlery and sinks; chisels need hardness.

options.text: Pure iron, which is ductile
options.explanation: Ductility helps shaping, not edge retention; the hard high-carbon steel is chosen.

check.stem: What is stainless steel alloyed with, and where is it used?

options.text: 20% chromium and 10% nickel, for cutlery, sinks and chemical plants
options.explanation: These are exactly the stainless row's composition and uses, prized for strength and corrosion resistance.

options.text: 0.25% carbon, for car body panels
options.explanation: That is mild steel's composition and use, not stainless.

options.text: 0.5-1.4% carbon, for chisels
options.explanation: That is high-carbon steel, the tool alloy.

options.text: 10% copper, for water pipes
options.explanation: No copper appears in the steel table; pipes are copper's own use.

check.stem: Why is iron chosen as a building material?

options.text: Good strength, malleability and ductility at a relatively low price
options.explanation: The building-material row lists strength, malleability, ductility and low cost together.

options.text: It conducts heat well, keeping buildings warm
options.explanation: Conduction is a saucepan property; buildings want strength and low cost.

options.text: It never corrodes
options.explanation: Iron rusts readily; the building case rests on strength and price, not corrosion resistance.

options.text: It is the lightest structural metal
options.explanation: Aluminium is the low-density choice; iron is chosen for strength at low cost.

check.stem: What single factor separates the three named types of steel?

options.text: The elements alloyed with the iron, especially the carbon content
options.explanation: Mild, high-carbon and stainless differ by what is mixed in and how much, which sets soft, hard or corrosion-resistant behaviour.

options.text: The furnace in which each steel was made
options.explanation: The type is defined by composition, not by which furnace produced it.

options.text: The country where the steel was produced
options.explanation: Origin plays no part; composition decides the type.

options.text: The temperature at which each steel is used
options.explanation: Service temperature is not the classification; the alloy content is.

glossary.definition: Able to be drawn out into wires without breaking.
Able to be hammered or pressed into shape without cracking.
A material that allows heat or electricity to pass through it easily.
Slow or unwilling to take part in chemical reactions.
The gradual eating away of a metal by chemical attack, such as rusting.
The iron alloy with about 20% chromium and 10% nickel that resists corrosion.

workedExample.prompt: a) Explain why aluminium is used for aircraft bodies and for overhead cables. b) Explain why copper is used for electrical wiring and for water pipes. c) Name the three types of steel with the composition of each and one use.
steps: a) Aluminium has a high strength-to-weight ratio (low density) for aircraft bodies, and it conducts electricity very well, suiting overhead cables.
b) Copper conducts electricity excellently and is ductile, making it ideal for wiring; it is unreactive with water, non-toxic and malleable, making it ideal for water pipes.

c) Mild steel (0.25% C, soft and malleable) for car body panels; high-carbon steel (0.5-1.4% C, hard) for tools such as chisels; stainless steel (20% chromium, 10% nickel, corrosion-resistant) for cutlery, sinks and chemical plants.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Low density + strength; good conduction. b) Conduction + ductility; unreactive with water. c) Mild / high-carbon / stainless as above.
